questions.corrige_markdown:
For Luke the miracles are signs that the kingdom of God has arrived and that Jesus is the Spirit-filled Messiah of the poor and the sick.

- *They confirm his mission.* At Nazareth Jesus applies Isaiah to himself: he is anointed to bring good news to the poor and to set the oppressed free (Luke 4:18-19). The healings that follow show this programme at work. When John the Baptist asks whether Jesus is the one to come, Jesus points to the blind who see, the lame who walk and the lepers who are cleansed (Luke 7:18-23).
- *They show the arrival of the kingdom.* "If it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you" (Luke 11:20). Miracles are the power of God overcoming evil.
- *They show compassion for outsiders.* Luke gives special attention to the widow of Nain whose son is raised (Luke 7:11-17), to the servant of a Gentile centurion (Luke 7:1-10), to the woman bent double healed on the Sabbath (Luke 13:10-17) and to the Samaritan leper who alone returns to give thanks (Luke 17:11-19). Women, Gentiles and Samaritans are therefore included in God's saving work.
- *They call for faith and lead to praise.* Many miracle stories end with faith and glorifying God.

The miracles are thus central to Luke's picture of Jesus as the compassionate saviour.

questions.corrige_markdown:
The Early Church treated the miracles of Jesus as proof of who he was and as a model for its own ministry.

- *Proof of the message.* In his speech at Pentecost, Peter describes Jesus as a man attested by God with mighty works, wonders and signs (Acts 2:22). The miracles were part of the first preaching and gave the apostles a basis for their claim that Jesus is Lord.
- *Continuing power in his name.* The apostles worked similar signs in the name of Jesus: Peter and John heal the lame man at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3:1-10), Peter heals Aeneas and raises Tabitha (Acts 9:32-43), and Paul heals at Lystra and at Ephesus (Acts 14:8-10; 19:11-12). Luke thus shows that the work of Jesus goes on through the church and the Spirit.
- *Growth and boldness.* These signs drew crowds, led many to believe and gave the apostles confidence when they were challenged by the authorities (Acts 4:29-30).
- *A model of care.* The church followed the example of Jesus in caring for the sick and the poor.

The miracles were therefore highly relevant: they supported preaching, strengthened faith and set the pattern for ministry.

The relevance of the miracles for society today may be seen at several levels, and Christians and others understand them differently.

- *Compassion and service.* The example of Jesus healing the sick, the lepers and the outcast has inspired Christians to build hospitals, clinics and schools for the poor, and to care for the sick and those with HIV/AIDS. In Cameroon, as elsewhere, many health institutions were founded by churches.
- *Hope in suffering.* For believers the miracles show that God cares about human pain and that evil, sickness and death do not have the last word. Many people pray for healing, and many churches hold healing services, though believers disagree about how far such healing can be expected today and about the risk of exploitation of the sick.
- *A challenge to exclusion.* The way Jesus touched lepers and welcomed the outcast challenges present-day stigma against people with disease or disability and calls for respect for every person.
- *Debate.* Some modern readers regard the miracles as symbolic, as signs of the power of Christ over evil rather than as events to be explained scientifically; others take them as historical acts. Both groups find in them a message about the dignity of the person.

The miracles remain relevant today as a source of compassion, hope and moral challenge.
